extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners / patent attorneys and disciplinary counsel (attorneys handling provisional/non‑provisional filings)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for evaluating a patent practitioner's professional conduct in preparing/filing provisional and design/utility patent applications and communicating with clients, as applied in a disciplinary proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable diligence and promptness
rubrics_metrics.description: "One of the highest duties of an attorney is to act with reasonable punctuality and promptness in advancing his client's interests and protecting his rights .... Procrastination and delay in handling of legal affairs ... may foster an impression ... that the highly‑vaunted standards of professional ethics are no more than a sham."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the practitioner prepared and filed applications in a timely manner given client expectations and circumstances. Consider explicit time commitments made to client (e.g., "one to two months"), the actual elapsed time to produce drafts/filings, the practitioner's estimates of typical drafting time (e.g., ~20 hours), and whether the practitioner took reasonable steps (including meeting with client) to meet agreed timing. Client urgency and poor finances increase the significance of timeliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decline representation if it will impair competent representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorneys have a duty to refrain from accepting representation if doing so will impair the attorney's ability to provide competent representation, to act with reasonable diligence, and to keep the client reasonably informed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the practitioner lacks resources/time (e.g., full‑time employment, long commute, only able to work nights/weekends) they must either decline the matter or ensure they can meet obligations; accepting work that will be pursued 'half‑heartedly' is an ethical violation. (Cited: State ex rel. Missouri Pub. Def. Comm'n v. Waters.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the client reasonably informed (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: "A practitioner shall: .. [k]eep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter." (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess communications (emails, phone calls, texts) and whether the attorney responded to or proactively updated the client. Repeated failures to respond to client inquiries or to provide promised drafts/updates (specific instances enumerated in the record) indicate violation. Patterns of unfulfilled promises about timing constitute failure to keep client informed.

rubrics_metrics.name: No false or misleading statements to client (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: "Professional misconduct for a practitioner to: .. [e]ngage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation." (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the practitioner made explicit promises (e.g., to email drafts, to file 'tonight') and then knowingly failed to perform or misrepresented status. A documented pattern of promising work and not delivering supports a finding of false/misleading statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional application purpose and minimal/formal requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional patent application is designed to provide a lower‑cost first patent filing, give an earlier effective filing date, and allow applicants to sooner describe their invention as 'Patent Pending.' A provisional does not need to comply with all non‑provisional requirements (e.g., abstract, oath/declaration, set of patent claims, or formal drawings); no Information Disclosure Statement is required since provisionals are not examined. (Citing 35 U.S.C. § 111 and MPEP § 601.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While formalities are relaxed, a provisional still needs a detailed and enabling description of the invention; the priority of a provisional extends only to information actually included in it. Practitioners should use the provisional as a tool to secure an early date and may defer more costly formalities for up to one year while preparing a non‑provisional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must obtain/seek enabling written description promptly if needed
rubrics_metrics.description: If additional written disclosure is needed to prepare an enabling provisional (e.g., flow diagrams, communication diagrams), the practitioner should request that information early on rather than delaying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to request necessary written description early, and thus failing to prepare a sufficiently enabling provisional in a timely fashion, is evidence of lack of diligence. The fact that an inventor may later provide materials does not excuse earlier inaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not parcel work in small increments to cause delay
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner should not unilaterally decide to request client information in small, incremental portions in a manner that prolongs the drafting process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the practitioner's method of eliciting information caused unnecessary delay, especially where the client responded promptly to requests. 'Step by step' incremental requests that extend the timeline can constitute lack of diligence when the client is cooperative and time‑sensitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not present or rely on new evidence / unauthorized expert testimony after deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: A party is not entitled to present or rely on new evidence or offer expert opinion testimony after the deadline for doing so has passed; offering unauthorized expert testimony in briefs is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Late additional factual assertions or expert opinions (e.g., about patent eligibility under Alice) that were not in the record may be disregarded and prejudice opposing parties who had no opportunity to rebut. Such filings should be ignored where deadlines have closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden to submit evidence when claiming diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: A party arguing it acted diligently must submit evidence to support that claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent documentary or testimonial evidence demonstrating prompt and reasonable effort, assertions of diligence are insufficient. (Citing Turner, 1991 Comm'l. Pat. LEXIS 5.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Client arrangements (e.g., client doing some drafting, payment delays) do not excuse practitioner obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreements that the client will assist with drafting (to reduce costs) or that the practitioner will perform work part‑time, or that payment is delayed, do not relieve the practitioner of the duty to act with reasonable diligence and to keep the client informed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the client consented to reduced scope or to doing parts of the work, the practitioner remains responsible for meeting timing commitments and ensuring an enabling filing. Payment disputes or the client's willingness to accept delays are not a justification for failing to perform or communicate.

rubrics_metrics.name: External legal developments do not excuse failure to act promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: Significant court decisions or guidance (e.g., Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank Int'l) that affect patentability require prompt communication with the client and appropriate action; using such developments as a pretext for delay is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely meeting with and advising the client about the implications of legal developments (and PTO guidance) is part of diligent representation. Delay in addressing the impact of such developments may itself be evidence of lack of diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional priority attaches only to information actually filed
rubrics_metrics.description: The priority date conferred by a provisional application extends only to the information included therein; material omitted from the provisional will not benefit from that earlier date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This legal consequence supports the obligation to include an enabling written description in the provisional and counsels practitioners to file sooner when necessary to secure priority for disclosed subject matter.
